17: **[Section 1 --- Purpose and Scope]{.underline}**
18: 
19: This document sets forth the standard negotiation positions, acceptable ranges, and walk-away parameters for Meridian Capital Securities LLC (\"Meridian,\" \"the Firm,\" CRD# 298417, EIN 83-2947561, LEI 5493007XKBT49LP2QR12) in the negotiation of Global Master Repurchase Agreements (\"GMRAs\") and Master Repurchase Agreements (\"MRAs\") with bank counterparties. All personnel on the Treasury & Secured Funding desk --- including traders, desk analysts, desk heads, and any other front-office personnel involved in onboarding or re-papering counterparty relationships --- and outside counsel (currently Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP, as further described in Section 13) must adhere to the positions and escalation procedures described herein. Failure to comply with these guidelines may result in disciplinary action, including but not limited to removal of negotiation authority and referral to the Firm\'s Compliance Department.
20: 
21: These guidelines apply to the following categories of documentation activity:
22: 
23: > \(a\) All new GMRA and MRA negotiations, including the drafting and exchange of Annex I (Supplemental Terms and Conditions) or comparable schedules, Eligible Collateral annexes, and any associated side letters or protocol adherence letters;
24: >
25: > \(b\) All material amendments to existing GMRAs and MRAs, including amendments that modify haircut levels, margin provisions, events of default, cross-default thresholds, substitution rights, repricing triggers, governing law, or dispute resolution mechanisms;
26: >
27: > \(c\) Any restatement or novation of an existing GMRA or MRA in connection with a counterparty reorganization, merger, or change of control;
28: >
29: > \(d\) Any side letter or supplemental agreement that modifies, supplements, or varies the terms of an existing GMRA or MRA in any material respect; and
30: >
31: > \(e\) Any documentation ancillary to a GMRA or MRA, including tri-party custodial agreements, settlement instructions, and netting opinions, to the extent such ancillary documentation contains provisions that interact with the substantive terms addressed in these guidelines.
32: 
33: For the avoidance of doubt, these guidelines do not apply to the negotiation of ISDA Master Agreements, securities lending agreements, or prime brokerage documentation, each of which is governed by separate guidelines maintained by the relevant desk or business unit.
34: 
35: The following foundational parameters inform the positions set forth throughout this document:
36: 
37: > • Meridian acts as Seller in substantially all repo transactions contemplated by these guidelines. The positions and ranges set forth herein are calibrated to Meridian\'s role as Seller. In the rare circumstance that Meridian acts as Buyer, the desk must consult with the General Counsel before applying these guidelines, as certain provisions (including haircut targets and substitution rights) may require adjustment.
38: >
39: > • The 2011 ICMA Global Master Repurchase Agreement (with 2011 Annex I --- Supplemental Terms and Conditions) is Meridian\'s standard form for cross-border bank counterparties, including all European, Asian, and other non-U.S. bank counterparties. The 2011 GMRA is published by the International Capital Market Association and is the market-standard agreement for cross-border repurchase transactions.
40: >
41: > • The SIFMA Master Repurchase Agreement (September 1996 version, as most recently amended) is Meridian\'s standard form for domestic bank counterparties --- that is, bank counterparties organized under the laws of the United States, including national banks, state-chartered banks, and U.S. branches of foreign banks.
42: >
43: > • Any deviation from the \"Acceptable\" range described in Sections 3 through 8, or any concession beyond the stated floors, requires escalation in accordance with the procedures set forth in Section 9. The escalation procedures are mandatory and apply without exception to all front-office personnel and outside counsel.
44: >
45: > • These guidelines are informed by Meridian\'s audited net capital of \$412,000,000 as of 31 December 2024, as determined in accordance with SEC Rule 15c3-1 (the \"Net Capital Rule\") under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended. All thresholds expressed as percentages of net capital are calculated on that basis and must be re-evaluated upon each quarterly net capital recertification. The Office of the CFO circulates quarterly net capital certifications to the desk, the General Counsel, and Risk Management within five business days following the end of each fiscal quarter. If a quarterly recertification reveals a change in net capital that would alter the dollar amounts implied by percentage thresholds set forth herein (e.g., the cross-default walk-away analysis in Section 7.1), the desk must coordinate with the General Counsel to determine whether an interim revision of these guidelines is warranted.
46: 
47: Nothing in these guidelines is intended to, or should be construed to, override or supersede any applicable regulatory requirement, including but not limited to SEC Rule 15c3-1, SEC Rule 15c3-3 (the \"Customer Protection Rule\"), FINRA Rules, or the requirements of any self-regulatory organization of which Meridian is a member.
48: 
49: **[Section 2 --- General Principles]{.underline}**
50: 
51: The following general principles inform the negotiation positions set forth in these guidelines and should guide the professional judgment of all negotiators in circumstances not expressly addressed herein.
52: 
53: **2.1 --- Overriding Objective.** Meridian\'s overriding objective in repo documentation negotiations is to maintain operational flexibility in collateral management while preserving robust netting and close-out protections. Operational flexibility --- particularly the ability to substitute collateral without undue delay or counterparty consent, to manage margin calls within reasonable timeframes, and to avoid unnecessary repricing events during the life of a transaction --- is essential to the efficient functioning of Meridian\'s secured funding business. At the same time, the integrity of netting and close-out provisions is critical to Meridian\'s regulatory capital treatment and insolvency protections. Negotiators must balance these two objectives and should not sacrifice one in pursuit of the other.
54: 
55: **2.2 --- Target, Acceptable, and Walk-Away Framework.** Negotiations should be conducted within the three-tier framework used throughout this document:
56: 
57: > • **Target positions** represent Meridian\'s optimal result and should be advanced in opening drafts. In the context of a first draft prepared by Meridian or its outside counsel, target positions should be reflected in the markup. In the context of a first draft received from a counterparty, target positions should be proposed in Meridian\'s first turn unless circumstances dictate that doing so would be commercially unreasonable or would unnecessarily prolong negotiations.
58: >
59: > • **Acceptable positions** represent the range within which the desk and outside counsel may agree to a counterparty\'s proposal without further escalation. Any position within the acceptable range is pre-approved for closing. The desk should exercise judgment in determining where within the acceptable range to settle; the midpoint of the range is generally a reasonable compromise and should be the desk\'s default counter-offer when a counterparty\'s opening position falls outside the acceptable range.
60: >
61: > • **Walk-away positions** represent hard limits. Acceptance of terms beyond walk-away thresholds is prohibited without Managing Director and General Counsel joint approval, which will be granted only in exceptional circumstances and only after a written assessment of the commercial rationale and risk impact has been prepared and presented to both approvers. Walk-away overrides are expected to be rare; if the desk finds itself seeking walk-away overrides on a recurring basis with a particular counterparty or class of counterparties, the guidelines themselves may need to be revised, and the desk should raise this with the General Counsel.
62: 
63: **2.3 --- Commercially Balanced Outcomes.** Meridian\'s reputation as a professional and fair counterparty is a significant competitive asset. Negotiators should seek commercially balanced outcomes and should avoid advancing positions that are unreasonable, one-sided, or not supported by legitimate commercial or regulatory concerns. At the same time, negotiators should not concede to a counterparty\'s position simply because the counterparty characterizes it as \"market standard.\" Market practice varies significantly by counterparty type, jurisdiction, and collateral class, and what is standard for a large European universal bank is not necessarily appropriate for a U.S. broker-dealer with Meridian\'s capital profile and regulatory obligations.
64: 
65: **2.4 --- Notice Provisions and Service of Process.** Negotiators should be mindful that Meridian\'s principal office is located at 200 Vesey Street, 38th Floor, New York, NY 10281, and its registered agent for service of process in the State of Delaware is Corporation Service Company, 251 Little Falls Drive, Wilmington, DE 19808. All notice provisions in GMRAs and MRAs should specify the Vesey Street address as Meridian\'s address for notice purposes, with copies to the General Counsel at the same address. Service of process provisions should reference the Delaware registered agent where the counterparty requires a U.S. domestic agent for service. Negotiators should not agree to designate any other entity as Meridian\'s agent for service of process without General Counsel approval.
66: 
67: **2.5 --- Confidentiality.** These guidelines are strictly confidential and are protected by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. No portion of these guidelines, and no description of the positions or ranges contained herein, may be shared with, disclosed to, or discussed with any counterparty, counterparty\'s counsel, or any other external party. Outside counsel is reminded that the existence of these guidelines and their contents are subject to the attorney-client privilege and must be treated accordingly. In the course of negotiations, outside counsel should advance Meridian\'s positions as Meridian\'s commercial and legal preferences without reference to the existence of formal negotiation guidelines or pre-approved ranges.
68: 
69: **2.6 --- Regulatory Awareness.** All negotiation positions and settlement outcomes must be consistent with Meridian\'s obligations under SEC Rule 15c3-1. Certain terms --- particularly haircut levels, cross-default thresholds, and margin provisions --- have a direct impact on Meridian\'s regulatory net capital computation. Negotiators are not expected to perform net capital calculations themselves but must be aware of the interaction between documentation terms and net capital requirements and must escalate any term that could have a material capital impact to the Office of the CFO through the procedures set forth in Section 9.
70: 
71: **[Section 3 --- Haircuts (Pricing Rate / Purchase Price Discount)]{.underline}**
72: 
73: Haircut levels --- referred to in certain GMRA contexts as the \"Pricing Rate\" or \"Purchase Price Discount\" and in certain MRA contexts as the \"Margin Percentage\" --- are among the most commercially significant terms in a repo agreement. The haircut determines the relationship between the Market Value of collateral delivered by the Seller and the Purchase Price received by the Seller. A higher haircut means the Seller receives less cash for a given amount of collateral, effectively increasing the Seller\'s cost of funding and reducing the efficiency of its collateral deployment.
74: 
75: For purposes of these guidelines, \"haircut\" refers to the percentage by which the Purchase Price is discounted relative to the Market Value of the Purchased Securities. All illustrative calculations in this Section assume a simple one-minus-haircut formulation --- i.e., Purchase Price = Market Value × (1 − Haircut) --- unless otherwise indicated.
76: 
77: **3.1 --- Sovereign Collateral**
78: 
79: Sovereign collateral is Meridian\'s primary collateral class for repo transactions and receives the most favorable haircut treatment from bank counterparties due to its high credit quality and deep secondary market liquidity.
80: 
81: **Target:** Haircut of 1.5% or lower. At this level, \$100,000,000 in sovereign collateral at Market Value produces a Purchase Price of approximately \$98,522,167.49 (reflecting minor rounding adjustments for accrued interest and settlement date conventions that may apply in practice). The 1.5% target is consistent with haircut levels observed in bilateral repo transactions between U.S. broker-dealers and well-capitalized bank counterparties during the period from January 2024 through September 2024.
82: 
83: **Acceptable:** Haircut up to 2.0%. The desk may agree to any figure at or below 2.0% without escalation. A midpoint settlement of 1.75% is a reasonable compromise and should be offered as a counter when the counterparty opens at 2.0% or above. At 1.75%, illustrative sovereign collateral with a Market Value of \$100,000,000 yields a Purchase Price of approximately \$98,280,098.28 (subject to the same rounding and convention adjustments noted above). The difference between the target of 1.5% and the acceptable ceiling of 2.0% represents a range of approximately \$500,000 in funding efficiency per \$100,000,000 of collateral deployed --- a meaningful but manageable cost within the desk\'s trading parameters.
84: 
85: **Walk-away:** Haircuts above 2.0% for sovereign collateral are not acceptable. Any counterparty insistence on a sovereign haircut above 2.0% must be escalated per Section 9. In practice, a sovereign haircut above 2.0% from a well-capitalized bank counterparty is unusual and may indicate that the counterparty\'s credit or risk function has classified Meridian at an elevated risk tier, which should prompt a broader relationship discussion rather than a narrow documentation negotiation.
86: 
87: **Eligible Sovereign Issuers:** The following sovereign issuers are eligible for the haircut levels specified above:
88: 
89: > • United States of America (U.S. Treasury securities, including Treasury bills, Treasury notes, Treasury bonds, and Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities)
90: >
91: > • United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (UK Gilts)
92: >
93: > • Federal Republic of Germany (Bundesanleihen, Bundesschatzanweisungen, Bundesobligationen)
94: >
95: > • French Republic (Obligations Assimilables du Trésor, Bons du Trésor à Taux Fixe et à Intérêt Annuel)
96: >
97: > • Japan (Japanese Government Bonds)
98: >
99: > • Canada (Government of Canada Bonds, Canada Treasury Bills)
100: >
101: > • Republic of Italy (Buoni del Tesoro Poliennali, Certificati del Tesoro Zero-coupon)
102: 
103: All eligible sovereign issuers must be rated A-- (Standard & Poor\'s) / A3 (Moody\'s Investors Service) or above by at least one of the two foregoing rating agencies at the time of the relevant Transaction. If the sovereign credit rating of any G7 issuer falls below the minimum threshold during the life of a Transaction, the impact on existing positions must be assessed by Risk Management in consultation with the desk. The inclusion or exclusion of specific sovereign issuers in Annex I is a material negotiation point and should be confirmed with the desk before finalizing any agreement.
104: 
105: **3.2 --- Corporate Collateral**
106: 
107: Corporate collateral is Meridian\'s secondary collateral class for repo transactions. Due to the higher credit risk and lower secondary market liquidity of corporate debt securities relative to sovereign collateral, bank counterparties apply larger haircuts to corporate collateral.
108: 
109: **Target:** Haircut of 3.5% or lower. At this level, \$50,000,000 in corporate collateral at Market Value produces a Purchase Price of approximately \$48,309,178.74. The 3.5% target is achievable with well-capitalized bank counterparties where the corporate collateral pool consists predominantly of investment-grade issues with short-to-medium residual maturities.
110: 
111: **Acceptable:** Haircut up to 4.5%. The desk may agree to any figure at or below 4.5% without escalation. A midpoint settlement of 4.25% is a reasonable compromise and should be offered when the counterparty opens at 5.0% or above. At 4.25%, illustrative corporate collateral with a Market Value of \$50,000,000 yields a Purchase Price of approximately \$47,961,630.70. The desk should note that the spread between the target (3.5%) and the acceptable ceiling (4.5%) is wider for corporate collateral than for sovereign collateral, reflecting the greater variability in market practice for corporate haircuts and the desk\'s need for additional negotiation room.
112: 
113: **Walk-away:** Haircuts above 4.5% for corporate collateral are not acceptable without escalation. Escalation must follow the procedures set forth in Section 9. Haircuts above 4.5% for investment-grade corporate collateral are indicative of an aggressive counterparty risk posture that warrants further review.
114: 
115: **Eligible Corporate Collateral:** Corporate collateral must meet all of the following criteria to be classified as Eligible Collateral under the GMRA or MRA:
116: 
117: > • Rated BBB+ (Standard & Poor\'s) / Baa1 (Moody\'s Investors Service) or above by at least one of the two foregoing rating agencies at the time of the relevant Transaction;
118: >
119: > • Residual maturity not exceeding 10 years from the Purchase Date of the relevant Transaction;
120: >
121: > • Denominated in USD or EUR (other currencies require General Counsel and Risk Management approval on a case-by-case basis);
122: >
123: > • Listed or admitted to trading on a recognized exchange or trading venue (for avoidance of doubt, securities traded exclusively on over-the-counter markets do not satisfy this requirement unless separately approved by Risk Management); and
124: >
125: > • Not issued by the counterparty to the relevant Transaction or by any affiliate of the counterparty (i.e., no \"wrong-way risk\" collateral).
126: 
127: **3.3 --- Haircut Negotiation Notes**
128: 
129: The following tactical notes are provided for the guidance of negotiators and outside counsel:
130: 
131: > \(a\) When negotiating with well-capitalized European bank counterparties --- in particular, institutions with Common Equity Tier 1 (\"CET1\") capital in excess of CHF 5,000,000,000 or EUR equivalent --- counterparties frequently open at 2.0% for sovereign collateral and 5.0% for corporate collateral. These opening positions are well-established within European bank playbooks and should be treated as the starting point for negotiation rather than as final positions. The desk should counter at Meridian\'s target levels (1.5% sovereign / 3.5% corporate) and expect to settle at or near the respective midpoints (1.75% sovereign / 4.25% corporate).
132: >
133: > \(b\) Certain counterparties may propose tiered haircut schedules that assign different haircut levels to different sovereign issuers (e.g., a lower haircut for U.S. Treasuries and a higher haircut for Italian government bonds). The desk may agree to reasonable tiered schedules provided that (i) all individual haircut levels fall within the ranges specified in Section 3.1 and (ii) the weighted average haircut across the projected collateral pool does not exceed the acceptable ceiling of 2.0%.
134: >
135: > \(c\) Haircut levels directly affect Meridian\'s net capital charges under SEC Rule 15c3-1. Haircuts materially above the acceptable range increase the capital charge on repo positions because the excess haircut represents a deduction from net capital. Any haircut level that would result in incremental SEC Rule 15c3-1 net capital charges in excess of \$5,000,000 in aggregate across the projected transaction portfolio with the relevant counterparty must be flagged to the Office of the CFO before the desk or outside counsel conveys agreement to the counterparty. This escalation requirement applies regardless of whether the haircut level is within the acceptable range specified in this Section 3.
136: >
137: > \(d\) The desk should avoid agreeing to haircut \"reopener\" or \"reset\" provisions that allow the counterparty to unilaterally increase haircuts during the life of a Transaction upon the occurrence of specified triggers (e.g., a rating downgrade of the Eligible Collateral issuer or a market volatility event). Such provisions transfer pricing risk to Meridian mid-transaction and are operationally disruptive. If a counterparty insists on a haircut reset mechanism, the desk should propose instead that any increased haircut apply only to new Transactions entered into after the trigger event, not to existing Transactions.
138: 
139: **[Section 4 --- Margin Provisions]{.underline}**
140: 
141: Margin provisions govern the mechanics of collateral adjustments during the life of a Transaction and are central to both parties\' credit protection. The key margin provisions addressed in this Section are the Margin Threshold (the de minimis amount below which margin calls need not be made), margin call timing and settlement, and the Net Exposure Cap.
142: 
143: **4.1 --- Margin Thresholds (Delivery Amounts)**
144: 
145: The Margin Threshold (sometimes referred to as the \"Minimum Transfer Amount\" or \"Delivery Amount Threshold\") is the minimum Net Exposure that must exist before either party is obligated to deliver margin. Thresholds that are too low generate a high volume of small margin calls that impose disproportionate operational costs; thresholds that are too high leave excessive uncollateralized exposure.
146: 
147: **Target:** \$500,000 symmetric --- that is, a Margin Threshold of \$500,000 applies equally to both Seller\'s and Buyer\'s obligation to deliver margin. The symmetric formulation is commercially balanced and straightforward to administer. At a \$500,000 threshold and an assumed average transaction size of \$250,000,000 to \$500,000,000, margin calls will be triggered only when Net Exposure exceeds a de minimis level, reducing operational friction without creating material credit exposure.
148: 
149: **Acceptable:** Asymmetric thresholds, provided the Seller (Meridian) Margin Threshold is no lower than \$500,000. In practice, certain bank counterparties --- particularly those with large settlement operations and automated margin call systems --- seek lower thresholds to minimize their uncollateralized exposure to non-bank counterparties. The desk may agree to a Buyer Margin Threshold as low as \$250,000 where the counterparty insists on asymmetry --- that is, a \$500,000 threshold for Seller (Meridian) deliveries and a \$250,000 threshold for Buyer (counterparty) deliveries. This asymmetric formulation benefits the counterparty by requiring Meridian to deliver margin at a lower threshold when the counterparty is owed margin, while preserving Meridian\'s \$500,000 threshold when Meridian is owed margin. The desk should agree to this formulation only if the counterparty provides a reasonable commercial justification and should note in the negotiation record that the asymmetry was conceded.
150: 
151: **Walk-away:** Any Seller Margin Threshold below \$500,000 is not acceptable without escalation. A Seller Margin Threshold of less than \$500,000 --- and in particular, thresholds of \$250,000 or less for Seller deliveries --- would subject Meridian to frequent small-value margin calls that impose disproportionate operational burden on Meridian\'s New York--based operations and settlement teams. The operational cost of processing and settling margin calls at low thresholds (including settlement instruction preparation, DTC or Clearstream delivery execution, and internal booking and reconciliation) can be significant in aggregate, particularly across a large portfolio of outstanding Transactions with a single counterparty. If a counterparty insists on a Seller Margin Threshold below \$500,000, the desk must escalate per Section 9.
152: 
153: **4.2 --- Margin Call Timing and Settlement**
154: 
155: The following provisions govern the timing and settlement of margin calls under all GMRAs and MRAs negotiated pursuant to these guidelines:
156: 
157: > \(a\) **Margin call cut-off time:** 10:00 a.m. London time (which corresponds to 5:00 a.m. Eastern Time during British Summer Time and 4:00 a.m. Eastern Time during Greenwich Mean Time). This cut-off time is Meridian\'s standard position and is designed to accommodate the operational schedules of both European and U.S. settlement systems.
158: >
159: > \(b\) **Margin calls received before the cut-off:** Any margin call received by Meridian before 10:00 a.m. London time on a business day must be settled on that same business day, subject to the receiving party\'s confirmation that the margin call is accurately calculated and that the required collateral or cash is available for delivery. Meridian\'s operations team targets delivery by 3:00 p.m. Eastern Time for margin calls received before the cut-off, consistent with DTC and Clearstream settlement windows.
160: >
161: > \(c\) **Margin calls received at or after the cut-off:** Any margin call received by Meridian at or after 10:00 a.m. London time must be settled on the next business day. This next-day settlement convention is essential to Meridian\'s operational workflow: margin calls received after the London cut-off typically reach the New York operations desk during pre-market hours, and same-day processing and delivery of collateral in response to late-arriving calls is not reliably achievable within DTC and Clearstream settlement windows.
162: >
163: > \(d\) **Do not agree to same-day settlement for calls made after the cut-off.** Meridian\'s New York--based operations cannot reliably process late-day London margin calls for same-day delivery. This is a firm operational constraint, and negotiators should explain to counterparties that the next-day convention for post-cut-off calls is necessary to ensure settlement integrity and avoid failed deliveries.
164: >
165: > \(e\) **Valuation methodology:** Market Value for margin purposes must be determined by reference to closing bid-side prices from a recognized pricing source (Bloomberg or Reuters) on the business day immediately preceding the margin call date. Mid-market pricing or offer-side pricing is not acceptable. Where the counterparty proposes an alternative valuation methodology, the desk should insist on bid-side pricing (which is more conservative from the Seller\'s perspective, as it results in a lower Market Value and therefore a lower likelihood of Meridian being required to deliver margin) or escalate to Risk Management if the alternative methodology could materially affect margin call frequency or magnitude.
166: 
167: **4.3 --- Net Exposure Cap**
168: 
169: **Standard position:** \$1,500,000,000 Net Exposure Cap. This cap represents the maximum aggregate Net Exposure that Meridian may have to any single counterparty across all outstanding Transactions under a GMRA or MRA before Meridian is required to cease entering into new Transactions with that counterparty (or, in certain formulations, before either party may decline to enter into new Transactions).
170: 
171: This cap is non-negotiable at the desk level. It has been approved by Risk Management and the Office of the CFO following a comprehensive analysis of Meridian\'s counterparty concentration limits, net capital adequacy, and stress-test results under a range of market scenarios. Any request by a counterparty to increase the cap --- or any proposal by the desk to increase the cap in light of a particular trading opportunity --- must be escalated to the Chief Risk Officer. Requests to increase the Net Exposure Cap must be accompanied by (a) a description of the commercial rationale, (b) an updated counterparty credit assessment from Risk Management, and (c) a net capital impact analysis from the Office of the CFO.
172: 
173: The Net Exposure Cap should be expressed in the GMRA or MRA as a hard cap denominated in USD. The desk should not agree to formulations that express the cap as a percentage of collateral value, as a \"soft\" or \"guideline\" limit that permits temporary exceedances, or as a limit that applies only to margin-adjusted exposure rather than gross exposure. The \$1,500,000,000 figure must be clearly stated in Annex I or the applicable schedule and should not be subject to adjustment by reference to market conditions, collateral quality, or other variable factors without an amendment approved through the escalation procedures described in Section 9.
174: 
175: **[Section 5 --- Substitution of Collateral]{.underline}**
176: 
177: Substitution rights are among the most important provisions in a GMRA or MRA from Meridian\'s perspective as Seller. The ability to substitute collateral --- that is, to deliver replacement Purchased Securities and receive back the original Purchased Securities during the life of a Transaction --- is essential to Meridian\'s collateral management and portfolio optimization functions. Without adequate substitution rights, collateral pledged under a repo is effectively trapped for the duration of the Transaction, limiting Meridian\'s ability to respond to changing market conditions, client demand, or internal portfolio rebalancing needs.
178: 
179: **5.1 --- Substitution Rights**
180: 
181: **Target:** Unilateral right of substitution by Seller on 1 business day\'s prior notice to Buyer, without requirement for Buyer consent. Under this formulation, Meridian may deliver substitute collateral of equivalent or greater Market Value and receive back the original Purchased Securities, subject only to the condition that Meridian provide at least one full business day\'s advance written notice of the substitution. No conditions beyond the notice requirement would apply --- Meridian would have full discretion to determine the composition of substitute collateral, subject only to the requirement that the substitute collateral constitute Eligible Collateral under the terms of Annex I. This target position maximizes Meridian\'s operational flexibility and is commercially appropriate in transactions where the Buyer\'s economic interest is in the repo rate rather than in the specific identity of the collateral.
182: 
183: **Acceptable:** Seller\'s right of substitution on 1 business day\'s notice, subject to the following conditions:
184: 
185: > \(a\) Substitute collateral must fall within the same or a better Eligible Collateral category as the original Purchased Securities. For purposes of this condition, sovereign collateral is a \"better\" category than corporate collateral. Accordingly, substitution of sovereign collateral for corporate collateral is permitted (a substitution \"up\"), but substitution of corporate collateral for sovereign collateral is not permitted (a substitution \"down\"). This condition protects the Buyer against collateral quality deterioration during the life of the Transaction while preserving Meridian\'s ability to manage its collateral inventory within a given quality tier.
186: >
187: > \(b\) No Margin Deficit exists at the time of the proposed substitution. This condition ensures that Meridian is not using the substitution mechanism to avoid or defer a margin call. If a Margin Deficit exists, Meridian must first satisfy the margin call and then, once the Margin Deficit has been eliminated, may exercise its substitution right. This is a reasonable condition that aligns the incentives of both parties.
188: >
189: > \(c\) No prior consent of Buyer is required. This is a critical element of the acceptable formulation. The distinction between a substitution right that is subject to conditions (acceptable) and a substitution right that requires Buyer consent (not acceptable) is fundamental. A conditional substitution right preserves Meridian\'s control over the timing and execution of the substitution; a consent-based substitution right transfers that control to the Buyer and introduces the risk of delay or refusal, which is operationally unacceptable.
190: 
191: **Walk-away:** Any requirement for Buyer\'s prior written consent to substitution is unacceptable. Such a provision effectively converts the repo into a pledge structure from an operational perspective, even if the legal characterization as a sale and repurchase is preserved. If the Buyer must consent before Meridian can substitute collateral, Meridian\'s collateral management team cannot reliably plan or execute portfolio rebalancing, and the practical utility of the substitution right is severely impaired. The desk must not agree to a consent requirement under any circumstances without escalation to the Managing Director and the General Counsel under the walk-away override procedures described in Section 9.3.
192: 
193: If a counterparty insists on consent rights, the desk should explain that the \"same-or-better\" collateral quality condition and the \"no Margin Deficit\" condition described above adequately protect the Buyer\'s interests. The Buyer\'s credit exposure is unaffected by a substitution that delivers collateral of equivalent or better quality and value, and the Buyer\'s protection against undercollateralization is preserved by the no-Margin-Deficit condition. Consent mechanisms introduce unacceptable operational delay --- particularly in cross-border transactions where the Buyer\'s credit and operations teams may be in different time zones from Meridian\'s operations desk --- and serve no legitimate protective function that is not already addressed by the two conditions described above.
194: 
195: **5.2 --- Negotiation Notes**
196: 
197: The following tactical notes are provided for the guidance of negotiators and outside counsel:
198: 
199: > \(a\) European bank counterparties commonly open by requiring Buyer\'s prior written consent to any substitution. This is a standard opening position in European bank playbooks and should not be treated as a walk-away trigger for the negotiation as a whole. Instead, the desk should counter with the acceptable formulation described in Section 5.1 (conditional substitution without consent) and explain the commercial rationale. In the experience of the desk, most European bank counterparties will ultimately accept the conditional formulation after one or two rounds of negotiation.
200: >
201: > \(b\) Some counterparties may propose a middle ground in which consent is required only for substitutions that involve a change in collateral category (e.g., from sovereign to corporate) but not for substitutions within the same category. This middle ground may appear reasonable but is unnecessary if the \"same-or-better\" condition is in place, as that condition already prohibits downward substitutions. The desk should point this out and insist on the clean conditional formulation without any consent overlay.
202: >
203: > \(c\) The 1 business day notice period is operationally critical. It provides Meridian\'s operations team with sufficient lead time to coordinate with the relevant settlement systems --- The Depository Trust Company (\"DTC\") for USD-denominated collateral and Clearstream Banking S.A. for EUR-denominated collateral --- to prepare and execute the simultaneous delivery of substitute collateral and receipt of original collateral. A shorter notice period (e.g., same-day notice) may not provide adequate time for settlement instruction preparation and execution, particularly for EUR-denominated collateral settling through Clearstream, which operates on Central European Time. A longer notice period (e.g., 2 or more business days) may be acceptable if the counterparty insists but reduces Meridian\'s agility in managing its collateral book and should not be offered proactively.
204: >
205: > \(d\) The desk should ensure that the substitution mechanics in Annex I are drafted to provide for \"simultaneous exchange\" --- that is, the delivery of substitute collateral and the return of original collateral should occur on the same settlement date and, where possible, through delivery-versus-delivery (DVP) or free-of-payment (FOP) mechanisms that minimize settlement risk for both parties. The desk should not agree to formulations that require Meridian to deliver substitute collateral one or more settlement cycles before receiving back the original collateral, as this would create a \"gap\" period during which Meridian has outstanding deliveries on both sides of the substitution.
206: 
207: **[Section 6 --- Repricing]{.underline}**
208: 
209: Repricing provisions allow one or both parties to adjust the Purchase Price of an outstanding Transaction to reflect changes in the Market Value of the Purchased Securities or changes in prevailing market repo rates during the Transaction\'s term. From Meridian\'s perspective as Seller, in-term repricing introduces operational complexity and potential P&L volatility, particularly where repricing triggers a cash payment obligation (either a payment by Meridian to the counterparty if the Market Value of the collateral has declined, or a return of cash by the counterparty to Meridian if the Market Value has increased). The desk\'s objective is to minimize repricing frequency while acknowledging that bank counterparties with term repo exposures have a legitimate interest in periodic repricing to manage their balance-sheet exposure.
210: 
211: **6.1 --- Repricing Rights**
212: 
213: **Target:** Repricing available only at maturity roll --- that is, no in-term repricing right for either party during the life of an individual Transaction. Under this formulation, the Purchase Price set at the inception of a Transaction would remain fixed throughout the Transaction\'s term, and any adjustment to pricing would occur only when the Transaction matures and is rolled into a new Transaction (if applicable). This target position eliminates the operational burden of in-term repricing and provides Meridian with pricing certainty for the duration of each Transaction.
214: 
215: **Acceptable:** Quarterly repricing or repricing on the 90th calendar day from the Purchase Date, whichever occurs later, with no less than 2 business days\' prior written notice by the requesting party. The desk may agree to either a quarterly cycle (i.e., repricing on the 91st, 182nd, and 273rd calendar day from the Purchase Date, or the next business day if such date falls on a non-business day) or a 90-day cycle (i.e., repricing on each 90th calendar day from the Purchase Date). Where the counterparty proposes both triggers --- for example, repricing on each calendar quarter-end *and* on each 90th calendar day --- the \"whichever is later\" formulation ensures that Meridian is not subject to repricing more frequently than quarterly. The desk should insist on this qualifier in all cases where both triggers are proposed.
216: 
217: The 2 business day notice period is a critical element of the acceptable formulation. It provides Meridian\'s operations team with adequate time to source replacement collateral, adjust positions, prepare cash for any repricing payment, and coordinate with settlement systems. The 2 business day period also allows for at least one full business day of internal processing after receipt of the repricing notice, accounting for the possibility that the notice is received near end-of-day.
218: 
219: **Walk-away:** Any repricing frequency more often than quarterly --- including but not limited to monthly repricing, bi-weekly repricing, weekly repricing, or on-demand repricing at the counterparty\'s sole discretion --- is not acceptable. In-term repricing at sub-quarterly frequency imposes significant operational and P&L volatility on the desk and is disproportionate to the counterparty\'s legitimate risk management needs. Sub-quarterly repricing must be escalated under the walk-away procedures described in Section 9, and approval is expected to be granted only in extraordinary circumstances (e.g., a transaction with an unusually long tenor and unusual collateral characteristics that justify more frequent adjustments).
220: 
221: **6.2 --- Negotiation Notes**
222: 
223: The following tactical notes are provided for the guidance of negotiators and outside counsel:
224: 
225: > \(a\) Bank counterparties conducting term trades in excess of 60 calendar days will uniformly resist Meridian\'s target of repricing only at maturity roll. The desk should expect to concede this point early in the negotiation and move promptly to the acceptable position. Protracted insistence on the \"repricing at maturity only\" target in the face of clear counterparty resistance is unlikely to be productive and may consume negotiation capital that is better deployed on other issues.
226: >
227: > \(b\) The critical protection for Meridian in the acceptable position is the 2 business day notice period. This notice period provides adequate time for the desk to source replacement collateral, calculate and prepare any cash payment, and execute settlement instructions. Do not agree to notice periods shorter than 2 business days under any circumstances. A 1 business day notice period --- or, worse, a \"same-day\" notice period --- would compress Meridian\'s operational response time below acceptable levels, particularly for repricing events that involve EUR-denominated collateral settling through Clearstream.
228: >
229: > \(c\) Where the counterparty\'s opening position is a 90th calendar day repricing option (as is common under European bank playbooks, particularly for Swiss and German bank counterparties), a reasonable compromise is to accept the 90th day trigger but add the quarterly alternative, with the \"whichever is later\" qualifier, to smooth timing and ensure that repricing does not occur more frequently than once per quarter. This compromise gives the counterparty its preferred 90-day trigger while protecting Meridian against the possibility that the 90-day cycle and the quarterly cycle could produce overlapping repricing events in quick succession.
230: >
231: > \(d\) The desk should be aware that some counterparties may propose repricing triggers that are linked to external events rather than fixed time periods --- for example, repricing upon a credit downgrade of the Eligible Collateral issuer, a specified decline in the Market Value of the collateral, or a significant move in benchmark repo rates. Such event-driven repricing triggers are generally unacceptable because they introduce uncertainty about the timing and frequency of repricing and can result in multiple repricing events in a short period during market stress. The desk should resist event-driven triggers and should propose that the counterparty\'s concerns be addressed through the margin provisions (which already provide for collateral adjustment in response to market value changes) rather than through the repricing mechanism.
232: 
233: **[Section 7 --- Events of Default]{.underline}**
234: 
235: Events of Default provisions define the circumstances under which a party\'s obligations under the GMRA or MRA may be accelerated and the close-out netting mechanism invoked. Properly calibrated Events of Default are essential both to protect Meridian against a counterparty\'s creditworthiness deterioration and to prevent Meridian from being subject to premature or unjustified close-out by the counterparty. The two Events of Default that are most frequently the subject of negotiation are the Cross-Default provision and the Act of Insolvency grace period.
236: 
237: **7.1 --- Cross-Default**
238: 
239: The Cross-Default provision in a GMRA or MRA provides that a default by a party under any other agreement (typically, a default in payment of indebtedness above a specified threshold) constitutes an Event of Default under the GMRA or MRA, even if no default has occurred under the GMRA or MRA itself. Cross-Default provisions are a standard feature of GMRA and MRA documentation and serve as an early-warning mechanism --- they permit the non-defaulting party to close out and exercise its netting rights before the defaulting party\'s financial condition deteriorates further. However, the Cross-Default threshold must be set at a level that captures only material defaults; a threshold that is too low can trigger cascading defaults across Meridian\'s entire agreement portfolio in response to minor or technical payment failures.
240: 
241: **Target:** Cross-Default threshold of \$50,000,000 for both parties. At Meridian\'s audited net capital of \$412,000,000 (31 December 2024), \$50,000,000 represents approximately 12.14% of net capital --- a level that captures only material payment failures and is well above the range of routine mark-to-market fluctuations, operational payment delays, and minor settlement failures that can occur in the ordinary course of Meridian\'s business. The \$50,000,000 target is Meridian\'s preferred opening position and should be included in all first drafts.
242: 
243: **Floor (Acceptable):** \$25,000,000. This represents approximately 6.07% of Meridian\'s net capital. The desk may agree to any cross-default threshold at or above \$25,000,000 without CFO sign-off. A \$25,000,000 threshold is a reasonable compromise that still provides a meaningful buffer against cascading defaults triggered by non-material events. The desk should offer \$25,000,000 as a midpoint counter-offer early in the negotiation when the counterparty opens below the target, with the goal of closing on this figure and avoiding a protracted back-and-forth on the cross-default issue.
244: 
245: **CFO Sign-off Required:** Any cross-default threshold below \$25,000,000 but at or above \$15,000,000 requires the prior written approval of Meridian\'s Chief Financial Officer. Requests for CFO approval must be submitted in writing (email to the CFO with copies to the Managing Director and the General Counsel) and must include a memorandum setting out:
246: 
247: > \(a\) The counterparty\'s rationale for seeking a threshold below \$25,000,000 --- including any regulatory, risk management, or credit policy considerations cited by the counterparty;
248: >
249: > \(b\) The number and aggregate notional of existing agreements in Meridian\'s documentation portfolio with cross-default thresholds below \$25,000,000, together with a list of the relevant counterparties and the applicable threshold for each agreement. This information is necessary to assess the aggregate cascading-default risk across Meridian\'s portfolio --- if a material number of existing agreements already have low cross-default thresholds, the incremental risk of adding another such agreement is magnified;
250: >
251: > \(c\) The incremental SEC Rule 15c3-1 net capital impact, if any, of a lower cross-default threshold. While the cross-default threshold itself does not directly generate a net capital charge, a lower threshold increases the probability of an Event of Default being triggered, which could in turn require Meridian to take reserves or charges against its net capital computation in connection with close-out or unwind scenarios; and
252: >
253: > \(d\) The desk\'s recommendation, including any proposed conditions or mitigants (e.g., a higher threshold that applies only to Meridian\'s obligations, or a cure period that applies before the Cross-Default is triggered).
254: 
255: **Walk-away:** Any cross-default threshold below \$15,000,000 is not acceptable under any circumstances. At \$15,000,000, the threshold would represent less than 3.64% of Meridian\'s audited net capital --- a level at which routine mark-to-market losses, minor operational payment failures, or ordinary-course settlement disputes could trigger cascading defaults across Meridian\'s agreement portfolio. The systemic risk to Meridian of a low cross-default threshold is disproportionate to the incremental credit protection it provides to the counterparty, particularly given that the counterparty\'s primary protection in a repo transaction is the collateral itself, supplemented by margin provisions. Negotiators must not agree to a cross-default threshold below \$15,000,000 even with escalation; this is a hard walk-away, and no override is available. If a counterparty refuses to accept a threshold at or above \$15,000,000, the desk should inform the General Counsel and the Managing Director, and the negotiation should be paused pending a senior-level commercial discussion about whether the counterparty relationship can proceed on other terms.
256: 
257: **7.2 --- Cross-Default Negotiation Notes**
258: 
259: The following tactical notes are provided for the guidance of negotiators and outside counsel:
260: 
261: > \(a\) European bank counterparties with large CET1 capital bases --- for example, Voss Bank AG, which reported CET1 of CHF 8,300,000,000 as of 31 December 2024 --- routinely propose low cross-default thresholds, often in the range of \$10,000,000 to \$15,000,000. The rationale cited by such counterparties is that these amounts are immaterial relative to their own balance sheets and that their standard credit playbooks require low thresholds for non-bank counterparties. The desk should explain to such counterparties that the cross-default threshold must be calibrated to Meridian\'s capital base, not the counterparty\'s. A \$10,000,000 threshold that is immaterial to a bank with CHF 8,300,000,000 in CET1 capital is manifestly not immaterial to a broker-dealer with \$412,000,000 in net capital, and the cascading-default risk of a \$10,000,000 threshold is borne entirely by Meridian. This is a straightforward and well-understood argument, and most European bank counterparties will accept it when presented clearly and early in the negotiation.
262: >
263: > \(b\) Offer the \$25,000,000 midpoint as a compromise early in the negotiation to avoid protracted discussion on this issue. Cross-default threshold negotiations can consume disproportionate time and attention relative to their commercial significance, and the desk is better served by closing on this point quickly at \$25,000,000 and reserving its negotiation capital for issues such as substitution rights and repricing.
